tldr: We proposed STRIDER, a hierarchical framework for humanoid robots that integrates continuous velocity-based walking with discrete, high-precision 3D foothold stepping, combined with upper-body manipulation. Using LD-PPO, a novel distillation method that merges expert policies of heterogeneous gaits into a single student policy, the system achieves accurate foothold placement and end-effector tracking on real hardware.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of STRIDER. On the left, individual experts for upper-body tracking, AMP walking, and 3D foothold stepping are pre-trained. In the center, LD-PPO distills the two lower-body gaits into a single student policy. On the right, during deployment on hardware, the robot executes upper-body tasks while seamlessly switching between walking and stepping according to high-level commands.
overview:
Loco-manipulation, where a humanoid robot performs tasks while moving, has been actively researched in recent years because it provides a much wider workspace than fixed robotic arms. However, most existing methods control foot movement through continuous velocity commands (forward/backward, sideways, and yaw turning). While this is convenient for traversing open spaces, it cannot specify pinpoint foot placement when approaching a target—such as placing the right foot a few centimeters further forward and turned slightly outward. Consequently, subtle discrepancies in stance right before manipulation can leave targets out of reach or compromise stability.

To solve this, the authors devised STRIDER, a hierarchical framework that combines natural velocity-based walking for long-range locomotion, discrete 3D stepping for precise foot placement right before task execution, and Cartesian end-effector tracking for the upper body. By selecting safe footholds based on terrain irregularities and generating clearance-aware swing trajectories, the robot can place its feet accurately even on uneven terrain such as stairs and stepping stones.

The core technical challenge was how to merge two lower-body expert policies with fundamentally different characteristics—continuous walking and discrete stepping—into a single executable student policy for hardware deployment. Because simple action imitation (distillation) tends to disrupt coordination, the authors developed LD-PPO, a new distillation algorithm that explicitly aligns the latent skill representations with those of the teacher.

Evaluations in simulation and on the full-sized TianGong Omni humanoid demonstrated that LD-PPO substantially reduces foothold placement errors, stably enabling real-world stair climbing while carrying loads, stepping-stone traversal, and workstation approach and manipulation.
contributions: Proposed STRIDER, a hierarchical loco-manipulation framework integrating high-precision 3D stepping, natural velocity-based walking, base posture control, and Cartesian upper-body manipulation.

Constructed a terrain-adaptive 3D foothold controller combining a stance-foot frame command system, three safety evaluation filters based on foot size, and Bézier curves for clearance-aware swing trajectories.

Proposed LD-PPO, a latent distillation method that learns latent coordination representations from teacher state-action pairs and reconstructs them from observations alone, improving the fusion accuracy of heterogeneous gaits.
Demonstrated real-world hardware deployment on the TianGong Omni humanoid, including stepping-stone traversal, stair climbing, and load-carrying manipulation.

sections.heading: Why Velocity Walking Alone Falls Short: Fusing Footholds and Manipulation
sections.summary: Although reinforcement learning has advanced whole-body humanoid control, conventional loco-manipulation relies on continuous velocity commands, preventing precise foothold specification. This causes difficulties in pre-manipulation stance and stability. To address this, this work proposes STRIDER, which integrates discrete stepping, walking, and upper-body control.
sections.details:
For humanoids to perform practical tasks in complex environments, they need mobility to navigate wide spaces quickly, manipulation to handle end-effectors deftly, and coordination to maintain whole-body balance. Recent deep reinforcement learning has achieved striking results, ranging from acrobatic parkour to reaching motions that coordinate the arms and pelvis.

However, most current loco-manipulation policies drive the lower body via continuous velocity commands (forward, lateral, and yaw). While this approach is simple and efficient for navigating wide rooms, it cannot directly specify where, at what height, and at what yaw angle individual feet should be placed. As a result, when the robot approaches a desk or shelf, slight foot offsets can leave the pelvis at an unsuitable position or heading, leaving targets out of reach or failing to provide enough stance stability for lifting objects.

Meanwhile, existing research on high-precision discrete foothold placement (stepping) focuses purely on locomotion alone, lacking integration with upper-body manipulation or active torso posture regulation. In this paper, the authors propose STRIDER, a hierarchical framework that unites the strengths of both worlds: walking naturally using continuous velocity from afar, and stepping with discrete footholds right before task execution to secure an optimal stance.

sections.heading: The Intersection of Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation, Foothold Planning, and Policy Distillation
sections.summary: Existing loco-manipulation primarily focuses on velocity walking, making stance fine-tuning difficult, while foothold planning has remained isolated to locomotion. Distilling multiple skills has also been hindered by simple action regression. This study tackles these challenges across domains by incorporating latent alignment into distillation.
sections.details:
### State of Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Mounting arms on a mobile base provides a significantly larger operational range than fixed arms. Prior studies have proposed decoupled upper- and lower-body policies trained with external force curricula, methods combining whole-body motion generation, trajectory optimization, and reinforcement learning, as well as directly learned whole-body policies. However, almost all rely on continuous walking velocity commands, making it hard to directly command the final stance foot placement right before task execution to set up the base posture.

### Humanoid Foothold Planning
Placing feet at target locations has historically developed through model-based methods like Zero-Moment Point (ZMP) preview control and Model Predictive Control (MPC). Recently, reinforcement learning methods have also emerged, enabling traversal over sparse footholds. However, these are pure locomotion controllers, not designed to coordinate with upper-body manipulation tasks or active trunk posture adjustments.

### Limitations and Breakthroughs in Policy Distillation
DAgger and Distillation-PPO (D-PPO) are widely used to transfer knowledge from privileged teacher policies (with access to exact terrain geometry and disturbances in simulation) to student policies running purely on real-world observations. However, standard distillation methods focus primarily on point-to-point regression of target joint actions (torques or target angles). When merging skills with fundamentally different dynamics and contact timings—such as natural continuous walking and pinpoint stepping—minor joint-space errors directly lead to missed footholds or balance loss. STRIDER overcomes this barrier by introducing skill alignment in the latent representation space, beyond just action regression.

sections.heading: STRIDER Architecture: 3D Foothold Logic and Latent Distillation LD-PPO
sections.summary: STRIDER consists of three phases: pre-training, co-training, and hardware deployment. Stance-foot-frame 3D foothold filtering and Bézier trajectory generation enable stable stepping on uneven terrain, while the newly developed LD-PPO fuses walking and stepping experts into a single student policy with high precision.
sections.details:
### III-A Hierarchical Loco-Manipulation Framework
The STRIDER training and execution pipeline is divided into three phases:
- **Pre-training**: Three policies are independently trained: an upper-body end-effector tracking policy $\pi_{\mathrm{upper}}$ reproducing human motions from the AMASS dataset, a natural continuous walking expert $\pi_{\mathrm{walk}}$ using Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP), and a 3D foothold stepping expert $\pi_{\mathrm{step}}$.
- **Co-training**: While a state machine alternates between walking and stepping, the proposed LD-PPO distills the two lower-body experts into a single student policy $\pi_{\mathrm{student}}$. During this stage, the upper-body policy is also active in simulation, exposing the lower body to arm-induced oscillations and disturbances to foster whole-body coordination.
- **Deployment**: Foothold targets are generated from camera-based terrain perception and localization, sending commands to the hierarchical upper- and lower-body controllers to drive the robot.

### III-B 3D Foothold Tracking
To accurately place feet on uneven terrain, STRIDER introduces a dedicated command space and safety mechanisms:
- **Command and Reference Frame Design**: Commands are 15-dimensional: velocity (3D), base posture (height, roll, pitch, yaw; 4D), and target positions and yaw angles for both feet (4D each). A key design decision is defining foothold targets in the "current stance-foot frame" rather than the base (trunk) frame. In a base frame, torso wobbles during stepping cause target footholds to drift in world coordinates, destabilizing learning. Using the stationary stance-foot frame ensures stable tracking.
- **Terrain Filtering Mechanism**: To ensure target footholds are not on hazardous terrain (cliffs or steep slopes), a $3\times 3$ grid of sample points is placed around candidate locations taking foot geometry into account (Fig. F3), evaluated against three criteria:
  1. $C_1$ (Height Uniformity): Whether the entire foot sole rests on a relatively level surface.
  2. $C_2$ (Continuous Incline): Whether the surface is smooth without severe drop-offs, even on slopes.
  3. $C_3$ (Reachability): Whether the step height relative to the stance foot is within reachable leg kinematic limits.
- **Swing Trajectory Planning**: Quadratic Bézier curves govern swing-foot height trajectories. By linearly interpolating lift-off and touchdown points while adding a parabolic margin (clearance) mid-swing, the foot avoids unwanted terrain contact during both step-up and step-down transitions, landing smoothly (Fig. F5, Fig. F6).

### III-C Upper-Lower Body Coordination
The lower-body walking policy acquires human-like locomotion via AMP by matching leg joint motion features with natural motion capture data. The upper-body policy is trained to track the Cartesian position and orientation (quaternion) of both wrists relative to the pelvis.

### III-D Latent Distillation PPO (LD-PPO)
When merging two disparate experts—walking and stepping—conventional action regression (DAgger) struggles to preserve inter-joint coordination. LD-PPO addresses this:
- **Architecture**: The student policy adopts an encoder-decoder architecture. The student encoder infers a latent variable (skill representation) from deployable observations, and the decoder outputs actions.
- **Teacher Alignment**: The teacher uses a privileged autoencoder conditioned on both observations and teacher actions. This constructs a condensed latent space reflecting the teacher's coordination strategies (e.g., balancing and swing-leg strategies).
- **Loss Function**: Three losses are jointly optimized: the on-policy reinforcement learning loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}$, the DAgger action reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$, and the alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}$ (Kullback-Leibler divergence) matching student latent distributions to teacher distributions. This enables the student to infer the teacher's sophisticated coordination representations from observations alone.

sections.heading: Hardware Humanoid Validation: Foothold Accuracy and Multitask Performance
sections.summary: Using the full-sized TianGong Omni humanoid and simulation, the components of LD-PPO were ablated. LD-PPO reduced real-world foothold tracking errors by about 10% compared to baseline distillation, successfully executing hardware tasks such as box carrying, stair climbing, and stepping-stone traversal.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Training was conducted in Isaac Gym on a single RTX 4090 GPU (4096 parallel environments, 50 Hz control). Real-world experiments used the full-sized TianGong Omni humanoid. A head-mounted MetaCam EDU sensor (10 Hz) generated local elevation maps, while Manifold Odin1 localization processed on an NVIDIA Jetson Thor generated foothold commands in real time.

### IV-A Distillation Algorithm Ablation
To verify each component of LD-PPO, hardware comparisons were run under identical command sequences (averaged over 20 trials each), measuring horizontal error $e_{\mathrm{2D}}$ and 3D Euclidean error $e_{\mathrm{3D}}$ at touchdown:
- **Proposed Method (LD-PPO)**: Achieved the best precision with $e_{\mathrm{2D}} = 113.2\,\mathrm{mm}$ and $e_{\mathrm{3D}} = 136.6\,\mathrm{mm}$.
- **Without Latent Alignment (w/o latent)**: Errors degraded to $e_{\mathrm{2D}} = 144.1\,\mathrm{mm}$ and $e_{\mathrm{3D}} = 169.0\,\mathrm{mm}$, showing that latent representation alignment is essential for transfer.
- **Without Encoder-Decoder (vanilla D-PPO)**: Yielded $e_{\mathrm{2D}} = 125.8\,\mathrm{mm}$ and $e_{\mathrm{3D}} = 150.5\,\mathrm{mm}$. The proposed method reduced horizontal error by 10.0% and 3D error by 9.2% relative to this baseline.
- **Without DAgger (w/o DAgger)**: 3D error catastrophic exploded to $467.3\,\mathrm{mm}$. Even with latent alignment, direct action supervisory signals remain indispensable for learning accurate foot placement.
- **Without PPO (w/o PPO)**: 3D error rose to $160.3\,\mathrm{mm}$, confirming the importance of RL fine-tuning on the student's own state distribution.

Interestingly, omitting DAgger did not dramatically degrade torso posture (roll and pitch) errors. This indicates that pinpoint foothold placement is harder to learn than posture maintenance, serving as a much more sensitive benchmark for evaluating distillation algorithms.

### IV-B Manipulation Performance
Evaluating upper-body tracking, mean absolute error (MAE) for wrist position remained under $2.7\,\mathrm{cm}$ in simulation and under $2.3\,\mathrm{cm}$ on hardware, with orientation errors below $14^{\circ}$, demonstrating high accuracy.

### IV-C Real-World Demonstrations
On the physical TianGong Omni, STRIDER demonstrated seamless execution across multi-stage tasks: traversing variable-height stepping stones, ascending and descending stairs while holding a box, and approaching a workstation via walking before taking precise steps to lower its base posture for manipulation.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: STRIDER successfully integrated accurate foothold placement, natural walking, and upper-body manipulation into a single hardware control system. Terrain-aware trajectory generation and LD-PPO skill distillation serve as the core pillars.
sections.details:
This paper presented STRIDER, a novel loco-manipulation framework for humanoid robots. By generating commands in the stance-foot frame and applying local terrain filtering, the system ensures safe and accurate 3D stepping. Furthermore, by developing LD-PPO to align latent representations from teacher state-action pairs, distinct lower-body walking and stepping skills were distilled into a single policy with high fidelity.

Experiments in simulation and on the real TianGong Omni humanoid demonstrated superior foothold accuracy over existing methods and verified diverse whole-body tasks coordinated with end-effector tracking.

takeaways: Combining velocity walking with pinpoint foothold stepping balances transit efficiency with stance stability right before manipulation.
Defining foothold targets in the stationary stance-foot frame rather than the base (pelvis) frame significantly stabilizes learning.
When distilling heterogeneous gaits or skills into one policy, aligning latent skill representations from teacher state-action pairs yields higher accuracy than pure action regression alone.
Foothold tracking is far more sensitive to cumulative joint errors than posture tracking, serving as a high-sensitivity benchmark for distillation algorithms.
limitations: Foothold candidate generation and safety evaluation still rely partly on heuristic thresholds (e.g., margins and height differences tuned to foot sole dimensions).
Although upper- and lower-body policies are co-trained, dynamic mutual compensation under large center-of-mass shifts from heavy payloads may have limits.
Hardware foothold error remains around 11 cm, indicating that further improvements are necessary for environments requiring millimeter-level precision, such as walking on narrow beams.
